STARTER SET - HOW TO USE THIS MODULE Tex.text:
Welcome to the Alien Evolved Starter Set module.

If you are new to the Alien RPG system make sure you check out the @UUID[JournalEntry.SkwfSOD5gNvLhaLv]{MU/TH/ER Instructions.} Journal which can be found in the Journals tab. This contains a quick guide to using the Alien RPG system.

Alien Evolved Starter Set

All you need to run a game is imported and organised into folders for each of the asset types.

You can rerun the import script at any time by going to Configure Settings> Module Settings and hitting the import button. Any existing assets will not be overwritten so it's useful if you accidentally delete something.

Scenes

Organised into two folders:

  • Alien RPG Mother Aids: contains general background images to share with players.
    The "ToM - Meeting Room" scene is designed as a "Theatre of the Mind" map to use as a staging area for the players while dealing with the narrative aspects of the scenario. There is an invisible wall across the lower part of the map.
    The PCs are placed here which allows them to access their character sheets, make rolls etc.
    The upper portion is for the GM to put NPCs giving the same control.

  • Alien Evolved Starter Set: 5 scenes for the Scenario.
    Each scene has light blocking walls and doors and FoW enabled to provide a more immersive experience when the players are moving around the map.
    All scenes have basic lighting on the crew areas but not in the duct areas.

Actors

Folders for PCs, NPCs and Creatures are set up as per the scenario with any necessary equipment or creature attacks.
For PCs & NPCs the Skill-Stunts rolldown (clicking on the spanners next to the skill) will show all the skill stunt options as per the rules.
Similarly clicking on the Talent name will show the details for that talent.

During the scenario you will need to provide the players with Agenda items.
These are stored in the Items folder (see below).

When needed the GM drops the respective agenda card on to the player character sheet.
The player can then read the contents by clicking on the name as with Talents.

Where PCs and NPCs have Items these are set to "Inactive" so will need to be activated (left mouse click on the item image) by the player/GM to be used.

Items

Under the Alien Evolved folder:

  • Alien RPG Weapons: all the weapons that come with the Starter Set.
  • Alien RPG Talents(Career): all the Talents that come with the Starter Set.

and Hope's Last Day - Personal Agendasall the agenda items for the Hope's Last Day scenario. These are dropped on to the players character sheets as instructed during the scenario.

Journals

Under Alien Evolved Starter Set Rules:
Starter Set Rules Core rules for the starter set Journal. This can be shared with players.

Hope's Last Day Journal entry for the scenario. Chariot Of the Gods - Scenario Folder contains:

Tables

The Starter Set builds on the table structure set up by the core system and adds new roll tables to the structure for Creature Attack tables, Critical Injury and Trauma tables.

You can access these directly but using the macros makes the game flow faster.

Remember when the results are displayed in the chat window and there is a "roll for attack" shown you can click on the dice image to display the number of successes.    

Recommended Add-on Modules

While not necessary to use the Alien system of this module I would recommend installing the following Add-on modules as they make the GM's job a lot easier:

  • Dice So Nice:
    Alien RPG supports 2 dice face types.

  • Quick Insert - Search Widget:
    Allows you to quickly search for assets and drag them directly on to the scene.

  • Alien RPG - Motion Tracker :
    The module installs a button just over the chat box that you can hit. When hit, the button will scan for the nearest active and visible tokens based on the selected token. This is still under development but is a really good effect to add tension to a scene.

Macros

The Alien system comes with 4 macros that will help you run the game smoothly.

These can be found in the Compendium under Macro>Alien. I suggest you right click and do an "Import All Content" to get them into your library.

  1. Alien - GM Dice Roller: Allows you to perform ad-hoc dice rolls. Uncheck the GM Only box to make the rolls public.
  2. Alien - Player Ad-hoc YZE Dice Roller: Make this available to your players. They need to have a token selected before running the macro.
  3. Alien - Roll on selected Mother table V10: provides a drop down listing all the Mother Tables available. Allows multiple rolls against the table and modifiers (+/- x to roll not additional dice).
  4. Alien - Roll on selected Creature table V10: same as above for Creature tables but no modifiers and all rolls are private to the GM.

Starter Set Rules.text:
WHAT'S THE STORY MOTHER?

“And behold a great dragon... his tail drew the third part of the stars of heaven, and did cast them to the earth.”
—Revelation 12:3-4  

SPACE IS VAST, dark, and not your friend. Gamma rays and neutrino bursts erupt from dying stars to cook you alive, black holes tear you apart, and the void itself boils your blood and seizes your brain. Try to scream and no one can hear you – hold your breath and you rupture your lungs.

Space isn’t as empty as you’d think, either – its frontiers are ever expanding. Rival governments wage a cold war of aggression while greedy corporations vie for valuable resources. Colonists reach for the stars and gamble with their lives – each new world tamed is either feast or famine. And there are things lurking in the shadows of every asteroid – things strange and different and deadly.

Things alien.

This is the Starter Set for the ALIEN roleplaying game – a universe of body horror and corporate brinkmanship, where synthetic people play god while space truckers and marines serve as hosts to newborn ghoulish creatures.

It’s a harsh and unforgiving universe and you are nothing if not expendable.

Stay alive if you can.

The ALIEN roleplaying game can be played in two distinct modes: cinematic play and campaign play.

  • Cinematic Play: A cinematic adventure emulates the dramatic arc of an ALIEN film. Designed to be played in a single or a few sessions, this game mode emphasizes high stakes and fast and brutal play. Conflict between player characters is likely, and you are not all expected to survive. In fact, most of your PCs probably won’t live to see the end of the adventure. A short but complete three-act cinematic adventure, Hope’s Last Day, is included in this starter set.
  • Campaign Play is designed for longer continuous play with the same cast of player characters over several game sessions. In campaign play, you create your own PCs, using the rules in the full ALIEN RPG Core Rulebook.

ROLEPLAYING ALIEN

EACH PLAYER IN THIS GAME – except one – takes the role of a player character (PC). You might be a space colonist, a space trucker, a marine, or something else. You decide what your PC thinks and feels, what they say and do – but not what happens to them.

It’s your job as a player to portray your PC and imagine yourself in their boots. Your PC is a person with feelings and dreams, just like yourself. Try to imagine – how would you react if you were in their place? What would you do?

The player characters are always the protagonists of the story. The game is about you. Your decisions, your story. >

The Game Mother

The final player is the Game Mother, or GM for short. She describes the ALIEN universe to you. She portrays all the people and creatures you meet during the game. Characters controlled by the GM are called non-player characters, or NPCs for short.

The game is a conversation between the players and the GM, back and forth, until a critical situation arises where the outcome is uncertain. Then it’s time to break out the dice – read more about that below.

It is the GM’s job to put obstacles in your path and challenge your PCs, forcing them to show what they’re really made of. But it is not up to the GM to decide what happens in the game – and above all, not how your story is supposed to end. That is decided in the game. That is why you are playing the game, to find out how your story ends.

Safety Tools

The ALIEN RPG is a horror game and getting a good scare is part of the fun. That said, this is still a game, and no players should be forced to deal with topics they find distressing in real life, or that make them feel unsafe at the table.

To make sure everyone is having fun and feeling safe, we recommend that you use safety tools before, during, and after the game. Examples of such safety tools are pre-game discussions about lines and veils for subjects that players want to avoid or keep off-screen, safety cards to be shown during play by a player to indicate that they feel uncomfortable with what is happening in the game, and post-game debriefings.

Always respect any player’s wish to raise a concern at any time during the game or even to leave the table if they want to. And don’t forget to take breaks. More information about safety tools in tabletop roleplaying can be found online.

SO WHAT IS A ROLEPLAYING GAME?

If you have made your way here without knowing what a roleplaying game is, congratulations! Welcome to a rewarding and creative hobby. Roleplaying is a unique form of gaming that combines tabletop gaming with storytelling. Roleplaying games give you a set of rules and let you create your own story with your friends in a way that books, movies, TV, and even video games cannot. If you need advice or ideas, there is a range of online groups for the ALIEN roleplaying game, including the official forum on the Free League website. Welcome.

PLAYER CHARACTERS

Your player character (PC) is your most important asset in the ALIEN roleplaying game. They are your avatar in the game world. They are your eyes and ears out there in the deepest dark of space. Don’t screw it up. Take your PC seriously. As far as you are concerned, they are a real person – and their fate is in your hands.

That said, don’t try to protect your character from every conceivable danger. The goal of any ALIEN game is twofold – go on a suspense-filled thrill ride and create a damn good story. For that to happen you need to roll the dice, both figuratively and literally. You need to take risks.

Character Sheets

To keep track of your character’s game stats, you need a character sheet. Five filled-in character sheets are included in this boxed set, for use in the Hope’s Last Day cinematic adventure. Before play, decide amongst yourselves who will play which character. If you can’t agree, roll dice to decide.

Attributes

You have four attributes that indicate your core physical and mental capabilities, rated on a scale from 1 to 5. Your attributes are used when you roll dice to perform actions in the game, and to determine how much damage and stress you can withstand.

  • Strength: Raw physical power and endurance.
  • Agility: Speed, body control and motor skills.
  • Wits: Intelligence, alertness and sharpness of mind.
  • Empathy: Charisma and ability to read and affect others.

Skills

Your skills represent the knowledge you have acquired during your life. They determine, along with your attributes, how effectively you can perform certain actions in the game. There are twelve core skills in the game, all listed in your character sheet. Skills are measured by a skill level from 0 to 5 and each skill is linked to each of the four attributes. Read more about how skills are used under MAKING SKILL ROLLS .

Talents

Talents are tricks, moves, and minor abilities that give you a small edge. They are more specialized than skills and make your character unique. The effects of your talents are pre-printed on the character sheets in this boxed set. The ALIEN RPG Core Rulebook includes a wide variety of talents.

Resolve

Life in space is lethal. More often than you’d like, you’ll find yourself under extreme pressure. In the game, this mounting tension is represented by your Stress Level . To keep your nerves in check, you need Resolve – a numerical rating equal to your Wits plus Empathy scores divided by two (rounding fractions up).

Health

Even if you keep your nerves in check, chances are that sooner or later you’re going to get hurt. This is tracked using your Health score. Health is reduced by taking damage. When your Health is reduced to zero, you’re broken and might die. Your starting maximum Health equals your Strength plus Agility scores divided by two (rounding fractions up).

Personal Agenda

You might be a team, but each individual PC in your group also has an angle of their own – a personal agenda. In cinematic play, the PCs’ agendas are predetermined by the adventure.

This boxed set includes an agenda card for each PC for each of the three acts of the adventure Hope’s Last Day. At the beginning of each act, the GM gives each player a handout with a new agenda for the act. The agendas are hidden, you should not show them to other players.

At the end of each act, the GM evaluates the actions of each PC. If you took any specific actions to further your agenda during the act, you are awarded one story point (below Stress Response ). If you have any story points left after the end of a cinematic adventure, you may bring one (1) story point to the next adventure with the same group (GM’s discretion), even if playing a different PC.

In the ALIEN roleplaying game, your PC can end up in direct confrontation with another PC. It’s up to the GM to call out when a player versus player situation escalates beyond the point of no return.

When the GM has “called PvP,” the players involved play out the current conflict to its conclusion. After that, the PC who has “turned traitor,” if they are still alive, becomes an NPC and is from now on under the control of the GM.

This means that you should think very carefully before acting against the common interest of the group, even if you think it’s in line with your personal agenda – it may cost you your PC. You are strongly recommended to wait until the third and final act of the adventure before taking such drastic action.

Gear

To survive the world of ALIEN, you need the right gear. Some common gear is listed on Gear . The character sheets in this boxed set already have gear listed on them. If you find new gear, you must write it down on your character sheet. If it’s not listed on your sheet, you don’t have it with you.

Encumbrance: You can carry a number of regular-sized items (weight 1 in the gear lists at the end of this journal) equal to double your Strength rating without problems. A regular item takes up one row on your character sheet.

Heavy & Light Items: Especially heavy or bulky items count as two or more regular items, and thus take up several rows on your character sheet. At the opposite end of the spectrum, light items count as ½ or even ¼ of a regular item, and several of these can fit on the same row on the character sheet.

Tiny Items: Items that are even smaller than light items are called tiny. They are so small they don’t affect your encumbrance at all. Tiny items still need to be listed on your character sheet.

Over-Encumbered: You can temporarily carry up to twice your normal encumbrance limit, i.e. Strength × 4 regular items. When doing so, your Stress Level increases one step every time you move in a stretch of STEALTH MODE or a round of combat (COMBAT & INITIATIVE ).

Consumables

Space suits have an air rating, weapons have an ammo rating, and some types of gear have a power rating. Collectively, these are called supply ratings and are tracked on your character sheet or using the supply dial in this boxed set.

Supply Roll: Sometimes, you need to make supply rolls for your gear. This means rolling a number of stress dice equal to the current air, ammo or power rating, up to a maximum of six dice. For every rolled, the supply rating of the item is decreased by one.

Air: Air supply is not tracked in this starter set.

Ammo: Most firearms have magazines with a supply of ammunition. After firing your weapon, make a supply roll. When your ammo runs out, you need to reload (Ammunition ).

Power: Some items require electricity to function. After each use, or as indicated by the item description, you need to make a supply roll. When the power runs out, the item cannot function.

NPCs: To avoid excessive dice rolling, we recommend that the GM does not make supply rolls for NPCs. Instead, the supply rating for NPCs is simply reduced one step each time a supply roll would be made. The GM is free to make a supply roll for an NPC when dramatically appropriate, however. &

MAKING SKILL ROLLS

Roleplaying is a conversation. The GM sets the scene, you describe what you do, she tells you how the NPCs react, you respond, and so on – back and forth. The story grows one step at a time, and everyone lives happily ever after. Yeah, just kidding about that last part. Not on the Frontier, you don’t.

Sooner or later, the shit – just like prisoner Murphy – hits the fan. Things come to a head, and a problem mounts that cannot just be settled by talking your way out of it.

That’s when you call upon your mad skills to make a skill roll. Just break out the dice and show Mother you know a thing or two.

Base Dice & Stress Dice

There are two types of custom six-sided dice for this game, each available in this boxed set: base dice (black) and stress dice (yellow). Both base dice and stress dice have the symbol on the 6 side. Rolling usually means that a positive effect of some kind is triggered, such as succeeding at using a skill. Stress dice also have the symbol on the 1 side. Rolling can trigger panic or other adverse effects.

When To Roll

The Hope’s Last Day cinematic adventure indicates when to roll for a skill, but the GM is also free to call for a skill roll in a situation she feels warrants it. We recommend against excessive dice rolling however, saving the rolls for dramatic and tense situations where something is truly at stake.

 Means Success

To use a skill, add your skill level to your score in the attribute linked to the skill, and grab that many base dice. Then roll all the dice together. For your action to succeed, you must roll at least one 6 ( on the custom dice) – if not, your action fails.

Stress Dice: If you have stress level 1 or higher, add this number of stress dice to the dice pool as well. If you roll a on one or more stress dice, you suffer a Stress Response .

No Skill Level? If you don’t have the skill required for the particular action you want to perform, you can roll anyway – simply roll a number of base dice equal to your attribute as well as any stress dice.

Modifiers

The rules or the GM can modify your chances, adding or removing base dice for you to roll. This is referred to as +1 die, +2 dice, etc., and conversely –1 die, –2 dice, etc. You can never go below one base die. Modifiers never affect stress dice.

Gear: Equipment can modify your roll, but not always. Sometimes a specific item is needed just to perform the action.

Helping

Up to three other PCs and NPCs can help you with a dice roll. Each person helping you gives you +1 die, but they need to be in a position to actually support your action in a concrete way. The GM has final say. In combat, helping someone uses up your full action for the round.

Multiple Successes

The more you roll, the better the result. In combat, that usually means more damage, but it can mean any number of bonus effects. The adventure text or the GM has final say on what extra can be used for. >

Other Rolls

The rules sometimes ask you to roll D6, D3, 2D6 and D66. D6 means rolling a base die and reading the number, ignoring any symbols. D3 means you roll a D6 and divide the result by two, rounding up. 2D6 means you roll two D6 and add the results. Another type of roll is the D66, which means you roll two D6s – consider the first die as the tens digit and the second die the ones digit. That gives you a result between 11 and 66.

The air scrubbers on the USCSS Miranda are offline and our roughneck Nat tries to repair them. With Strength 5 and skill level 3 in HEAVY MACHINERY, she gets eight base dice. She uses a maintenance jack for the job and her crewmate Jeffries helps her out, giving her +2 dice for a whopping total of ten base dice.

Failure

If you don’t roll any    , you fail to achieve your goal. The GM or the adventure text will tell you what failure means. You have one last chance if you really want to succeed – you can push the roll.

Pushing Your Roll

If you fail a roll, or need more    , you can choose to push the roll. This immediately increases your stress level one step, meaning you add one stress die to your dice pool. Then re-roll all dice not showing    . All dice count after the re-roll, including the ones not re-rolled.

Stress Dice: If you rolled one or more    on stress dice in the initial roll, you cannot push the roll.

Just Once: You can only push your roll once, unless you have a talent that allows you to push a roll a second time.

Despite good odds, Nat fails to repair the air scrubbers. She decides to push the roll, increasing her stress level to 1 and adding one stress die to her dice pool. She then re-rolls the ten base dice along with the stress die, now getting two    . She succeeds, and as a bonus effect for the extra    , the GM decides that she finds a strange icky trail leading into the air shafts ...

Non-player characters use skills in the same way as player characters, with the one major difference being that NPCs never push rolls. This means NPCs don’t have a stress level. The GM rolls dice for NPCs, but should only roll for actions that affect a PC directly.

“There’s no bloody way I’m three months pregnant.”
“Well, doctor, it’s not exactly a traditional fetus.”
Shaw and David  

Stress Response

If you roll    on one or more stress dice in a skill roll, a stress response is triggered. Roll D6, adding your stress level and subtracting your Resolve score before comparing the result to the table below. Your stress responses are removed by Relieving Stress . If you get a stress response that you already have, you instead gain stress level +1.

STORY POINTS

In a cinematic adventure, you can spend a story points to automatically get a    result on one base die in a skill roll. This can be done before or after pushing the roll. You gain story points by following your Personal Agenda . You can never have more than 3 story points.

Passive Rolls

Sometimes, the GM will ask you to roll for something you’re not even aware of – typically OBSERVATION rolls in stealth mode (STEALTH MODE ). Such rolls cannot be pushed, nor trigger stress responses. You still add your stress level to the roll. The GM can even make some passive rolls in secret.

Opposed Rolls

When facing an active resistance to your skill roll, you need to roll off against your opponent. In an opposed roll, you need to roll    more than your opponent to succeed. You can push the roll even if you’re the target of an opposed roll. Opposed rolls are used sparingly, only when indicated by the rules or the adventure text, or when deemed appropriate by the GM.

PvP: In the case of two PCs rolling off against each other, the active PC decides whether to push the roll first, and if so, re-rolls, then the passive PC decides whether to push or not.

Open Rolls: In opposed rolls where there is no clear active party, a tie means there is no clear winner of the roll. If this doesn’t work in the situation, break the tie randomly.

Captain Charlize on the USCSS Miranda is attempting to bypass Mother’s antagonistic actions by accessing her core in the mainframe. The GM says this is an opposed roll against Mother’s COMTECH skill level of 7 (the ship’s MU/TH/UR 7000 mainframe has no base attributes). Charlize has no COMTECH skill, so she’s just rolling four base dice for her Wits and four stress dice for the current stress level. Her roll comes up with one    , but the GM rolls for Mother and gets two    .
Charlize decides to push the roll, increasing her stress level to 5 and adding another stress die to her dice pool. She then re-rolls all dice not showing    , getting two more    for a total of three! However, she also rolls one   on a stress die. With a Resolve score of 4 and stress level 5, she rolls a D6 and adds 1. In a stroke of bad luck, she rolls a 6 for a total of 7. The captain messes up! On the brink of triumph, Mother takes control of the USCSS Miranda and her communications. As a result, Charlize gains +1 stress level.

SPACE & TIME

“Should be in and out in thirty minutes.”
Tyler   

Maps

Hope’s Last Day and other ALIEN RPG adventures are typically played out using maps of the starship, colony, or whatever location your characters happen to find themselves fighting for their lives in. Smaller overview maps as well as large, full-color detailed maps of adventure locations are included in this boxed set.

Tokens & Miniatures: To track movement on the map during stealth or combat, you use the cardboard tokens and the Xenomorph miniature in this boxed set. If you have access to more ALIEN RPG miniatures, you can use those as well.

Zones

The map is divided into zones. A zone is typically a room or a corridor, although long corridors and large rooms can be divided into several zones. Zone borders are indicated on the adventure maps in this boxed set.

Cluttered/  Open: A zone is either cluttered, meaning there are objects in the zone to hide or take cover in or behind, or open, meaning there are no such objects in the zone. Open zones are typically corridors and crawlspaces, but can also be empty rooms or other open spaces. The Hope’s Last Day adventure indicates which zones are open or cluttered.

Borders: A border between two adjacent zones is either open or blocked (by a wall or bulkhead). A blocked border can have a door or a hatch, as indicated by the map, allowing movement between the two zones. Corridors and crawlspaces are divided into several zones by doors or lines on the map.

Line Of Sight: Except for characters who are hiding or in full cover, everyone in the same zone has line of sight to each other. This does not apply to narrow crawlspaces like air shafts – there, other characters block line of sight (even friendlies). Open zone borders don’t block line of sight. A blocked border generally blocks line of sight even if there is a door or hatch in it – unless you’re actively standing by the doorway and peeking through.

Range

The distance between combatants is divided into five range categories. See the diagram below.

Measuring Time

In the ALIEN universe, time matters. Whether you are awaiting rescue on an alien world with Xenomorphs stalking you, or Mother is counting down to the imminent destruction of your ship, you need to keep track of time.

Three separate units of time are typically used in the game, depending on the situation at hand. See the table below. The exact duration of a round, stretch and shift can vary depending on the situation.

UNIT   DURATION   PRIMARY USE
Round   5–10 seconds   Combat
Stretch   5–10 minutes   Stealth
Shift   5–10 hours   Recovery

STEALTH MODE

“If you don’t stay quiet, we all die.”
Andy  

IN THE ALIEN ROLEPLAYING GAME, much of the thrill happens before the enemy shows itself and bullets start flying. A key part of the experience is exploring unknown locations, with enemies lurking in the darkness. In the game, this is represented by what we call stealth mode. Stealth mode is played out in stretches of time, each approximately 5–10 minutes long.

PC Movement

Movement in stealth mode is slow and careful. In one stretch of time, your character can move into an adjacent zone on the map (assuming the border is open or has an open door or hatch), scan for enemies, and get a superficial description of the zone from the GM. If you’re a team, you can move individually or as a group. The order in which PCs move is chosen freely.

Searching A Zone: If you want to examine something in a zone more closely, to search a room or access a data terminal, you may need to stay several stretches in the zone (or even a full shift), if the adventure text or the GM calls for it.

NPC Movement

In stealth mode, NPC movement is managed secretly by the GM each stretch, after your PCs have moved. Human NPCs follow the same rules for movement as PCs, while Xenomorphs may move one zone per point of Speed (Combat Rules ) each stretch. The order of NPC movement is chosen by the GM.

Active & Passive: The adventure text may tell the GM that enemies are active or passive. Active enemies are moving across the map, stalking you or trying to hide from you. Passive enemies are not aware of you and are most often stationary, until they spot you or are otherwise alerted to your presence. Enemies may switch from passive to active, or vice versa, as dictated by the adventure or the GM.

Hidden Map: To manage NPC movement, the GM uses the smaller version of the adventure maps in this boxed set, hidden from view by the box lid (or GM Screen, if you have it). On this map, the GM moves the NPC tokens, hidden from the players’ view. If the GM prefers it, they can track hidden NPC movement on a piece of paper.

Crawlspaces

Air shafts and other crawlspaces are a common feature in ALIEN adventures and present a unique challenge in stealth mode. Crawlspaces can run by the side of rooms and corridors, above them or underneath them (in which case just the outline is shown on the adventure maps).

Access Points: A crawlspace can be entered by one zone’s worth of movement at any access point marked on the map, just like entering any other zone.

Sealing Access Points: An access point can be sealed shut with a cutting torch. This is described in the Hope’s Last Day adventure booklet.

Detection

When you come within line of sight of an NPC in stealth mode, or vice versa, make a passive open opposed OBSERVATION roll. This means the roll cannot be pushed, nor trigger Personal Agenda . The GM will just ask you to roll OBSERVATION without telling you why, and roll for the NPC.

If one side wins the roll, they spot the other first and can choose to declare their presence, ambush their opponent (Surprise & Ambush ), hide in the zone (Hiding), or back out of the zone the same way they entered. Backing out of the zone in this situation is done immediately and does not count toward the normal movement in this stretch.

On a tied roll, you spot each other at the same time – draw initiative (Drawing The Initiative ).

Keeping Guard: If a person remains stationary in a zone for a stretch and does nothing except keeping guard, they gain +2 dice to OBSERVATION rolls to spot anything coming within line of sight.

DARKNESS

In dark zones with very dim lightning, OBSERVATION rolls for humans (and androids) are made with –2 dice. Xenomorphs are not affected. A flashlight will remove the effects of darkness in a zone.

Groups In Stealth Mode

When several characters moving as a group come into line of sight of another character (or group), all characters in each group get to roll OBSERVATION. Only the best roll on each side counts. For a group of NPCs with identical stats, the GM will typically make just a single OBSERVATION roll and apply the result to the whole group.

Hiding

A character can hide in a cluttered zone (not in an open zone). To hide carefully takes one stretch, and thus cannot be combined with movement or searching the zone – except immediately after a (won) OBSERVATION roll when coming within line of sight of an enemy (see Detection, above). In this specific case only, hiding is “free.” Items can also be hidden in a zone.

Finding What’s Hidden: When an enemy enters a zone with a hidden character, no opposed OBSERVATION roll is made. Instead, the enemy must actively search the zone for a stretch and make an OBSERVATION roll. If the roll fails, another roll can be made each stretch. If a hidden character is found, draw initiative.

Multiple Searchers: If several characters search a zone at the same time, they can make separate rolls or let one character roll, and the others help (Helping ).

Taking Action: A hidden character may, at their turn in the stretch, take action to move out of the zone, interact with something in the zone, or ambush an enemy. In all such cases, make an opposed OBSERVATION roll against all enemies in line of sight.

Nat and Hayes are checking out the abnormal engine readings on the USCSS Miranda while carefully looking for the unknown killer on board, moving zone by zone in stealth mode. The GM moves the killer on her hidden GM map. It is currently stationary in the engine control room.

After a few stretches, Nat and Hayes split up as the medic wants to look for a surgical kit. On her turn, Nat moves very carefully into the engine control room, where a horrifying Xenomorph lurks. A passive opposed OBSERVATION roll is made, and Nat wins! She takes a chance and decides to hide in the zone, under a control console.

Now, as Nat is hidden and the Xenomorph is not actively looking for her, it does not get to roll OBSERVATION again until Nat moves out of hiding. The GM decides that the Xenomorph moves on its next turn, quickly jumping into an air shaft. Nat is free to come out of hiding to check the engine controls.

Motion Trackers

A motion tracker, such as the M314 unit Gear ), can be used once per stretch. This does not exclude other activities during the stretch, but before the tracker gives any information a power supply roll must be made.

If still powered up, the motion tracker will automatically detect the presence of all NPCs within its range (four zones for an M314), even if not within line of sight – but only NPCs who moved in the previous stretch. NPCs who remained stationary in the previous stretch are not detected.

Tracker Pings: Mark the “pings” of movement from a motion tracker by placing tokens on the map. Such tokens are included in this boxed set. Detecting an NPC with a motion tracker does not mean that the PC has spotted it – it only means the players get an indication of where an NPC is present.

Hayes is in the Medbay when the Xenomorph enters the zone via an air duct access point. The GM tells Hayes to roll OBSERVATION but not why, and rolls for the Xeno herself. The opposed roll is a tie, and they spot each other at the same time! Stealth mode ends and combat starts.

Starting A Fight

When a PC spots an NPC or vice versa, stealth mode ends, and initiative is drawn (COMBAT & INITIATIVE ). Draw initiative even if the NPC is not obviously hostile – forcing PCs who act first to decide whether to attack or hold off. Also note that PCs can exchange initiatives with NPCs or each other on their turn (see Holding Off ). Combat can also be initiated by an ambush (Surprise & Ambush ).

Social Mode

When you stop to interact socially with NPCs, or just stop to relieve stress (Relieving Stress ) or chat among each other, stealth mode stops. During social mode, the GM estimates how many stretches pass and moves NPCs on the hidden stealth map accordingly. Social mode can also be used when you perform a task that takes more than a stretch to complete. When you start moving around on the map again, stealth mode starts anew.

COMBAT & INITIATIVE

“LET’S ROCK!”
Pvt. Vasquez   

WHEN THE ENEMY IS REVEALED, stealth mode is over, and combat starts. Combat is played out in rounds, each approximately 5–10 seconds long. At the start of each round, the first step is to decide who has the initiative – in what order the combatants will act during the round.

Drawing The Initiative

To determine the initiative, ten cards numbered 1 to 10 are used, included in this boxed set. Each player in the fight draws a random card at the beginning of each round, and the GM draws cards for NPCs.

The number on the card determines the order in which you act in the round. Card #1 acts first, card #2 acts second, and so forth until everyone has acted. Your place in the initiative order is called your turn. Your “previous turn” or “your next turn” can occur in the current round or the previous/next round, depending on if you’ve had your turn in the current round yet.

Place your initiative card by your character sheet so everyone can see the order in which each person acts. The GM puts their card (or cards) in front of them. When all participants have had their turn, the round is over, and a new round begins by drawing the initiative again.

Xenomorphs have a Speed rating and get one turn – and initiative card – per point of Speed. The GM can read more about this in the adventure booklet.

Hayes faces the horrifying Xenomorph in the medbay, luckily drawing the #2 initiative card. As the Xenomorph has Speed 2, the GM draws two cards for it, getting the #5 and the #7. Nat over at engine controls is not aware of what is happening and thus does not draw a card.

Hayes could hold off to let the Xenomorph make the first move but decides to keep his #2 card and act immediately. He spends his quick action running to a nearby comms terminal, and his full action to use it to scream for help, hoping Nat will hear him and get there in time. Now it’s the Xenomorph’s turn ...

Surprise & Ambush

If combat starts with an attack that the GM deems to be surprising, the attacker automatically gets the #1 initiative card in the first round of combat. The other combatants draw their initiative from the cards that remain. With several attackers, they get the lowest (earliest) cards to distribute freely. At the start of the second round, everyone draws the initiative as usual.

Ambush: A special type of surprise attack is an ambush, which is an attack on an unaware opponent. Ambushes are usually the result of stealth mode (STEALTH MODE ). An ambush also gives the lowest (earliest) initiative card to the attacker(s), and gives +2 dice to the initial attack(s), and the target(s) cannot defend against it or dodge it.

Holding Off

At your turn in the round, you can choose to hold off. This means that you swap initiative cards – and therefore places in the turn order – with another PC or NPC (or NPC group) whose turn comes after yours. They cannot refuse the trade and must take their turn immediately. You cannot swap initiative cards with someone who has already had their turn.

Note: All rules effects that are triggered “on your turn” (such as death rolls, see Critical Injuries ) are moved in the turn order when initiative cards are swapped. Your turn doesn’t happen until you use it.

Interrupt Actions: Quick actions that occur out of turn (such as defending or dodging) are not affected by holding off – spent quick actions still count as spent, even if you get a new initiative number. Even if you have spent two quick actions as interrupt actions earlier in the round, and thus don’t get any action on your turn, you can still hold off and swap cards when your turn comes – this can be useful to give another PC an earlier spot in the turn order.

Xenomorphs (XENOMORPHS ) with a Speed of 2 or more have multiple turns in a single round, and therefore draw multiple initiative cards. When swapping cards with a Xenomorph, you decide which card you want, as long as it comes after your current turn in the initiative order. Xenomorphs themselves rarely hold off.

To make things simple, particularly in large fights, the GM can draw a single initiative card for a group of NPCs. All NPCs in that group act on the same turn in the round. The order among them is decided by the GM. When a PC holds off to swap initiative cards, they swap initiative with the whole NPC group.

In the next round, Nat is aware of the Xenomorph and gets to draw initiative. Sadly, she gets the #9 card. The Xenomorph draws the #3 and #8, while Hayes – terrified and wounded but still alive – draws the #1 card. Hayes decides to hold off and swaps his card with Nat, allowing her to go first. She spends both her quick and her full action to move, running the two zones over to reach the medbay, just in time to face the Xenomorph.

Each round, you can perform one full action and one quick action, or two quick actions.

Full Action: This is typically an attack but can be anything you could reasonably do in less than 10 seconds that requires your full focus. It typically requires a skill roll. See the list above for examples. A full action can only be performed on your turn in the round.

Quick Action: These are faster and don’t necessarily demand a skill roll. Quick actions include movement. See the list above for examples. Some quick actions can be performed out of turn, to interrupt the actions of opponents. On your turn, you can save your quick action for an interrupt action to use later in the round. If you perform two quick actions in the same round, you forfeit your full action.

Action Reset: All actions are reset at the start of a new combat round. Actions can never be saved from one round to the next. >

Giving Orders

As a full action, you can bark orders to another character. They must be able to hear you, even if via comms. Roll for COMMAND. For every you roll, they get +1 die to one roll later in the same round, but only for carrying out the order you gave.

Foot Movement

To move during combat, you can spend a quick action to go from one zone to an adjacent zone, to move up to a door or hatch to peek through it (or take cover by it), or to move between Short and Adjacent range from a character (or item) inside your current zone.

Doors & Hatches: You can pass an unlocked door or hatch during movement without spending an action. Locking a door or hatch is a quick action. A locked door or hatch can be broken down. This requires a close combat attack (full action) with +2 dice. A typical metal door or hatch has armor level 2 and can take 10 points of damage before it gives in. Electronically locked doors or hatches can be opened with a COMTECH roll (full action).

Blocking Movement: You can block another character from moving past you. As a rule of thumb, you can block a cylindrical volume 2 meters wide and equally tall. To pass you, your opponent must either take you out or make a special close combat action (below). Blocking is not mandatory – you can allow friendly characters to pass you.

If you are using official ALIEN RPG tokens or miniatures on a map that is to scale, mark Adjacent range by placing the tokens or miniature bases in contact. If there is no way to move into a zone without placing the tokens or miniatures in contact, the range between them is immediately Adjacent (not Short), without a further move action needed.
You can move into a narrow area on the map (such as a crawlspace) even if your token or miniature base is wider than the space you’re in. However, if the tokens /miniatures of other characters make it impossible to place at least half of your token / base inside a zone (GM’s call), you cannot move into it. Broken characters don’t count.
You can block movement in an area covered by the token or the base of the miniature. Several characters can be placed in base-to-base contact to block wider areas.

MARK YOUR ACTIONS

To keep track of your actions in the round, a tip is to keep your initiative face-up and vertical at the start of the round. Turn it horizontally when you perform a quick action. Flip the card over when you perform a full action or your second quick action. When the card is both rotated and flipped, you’re done for the round!

Crawlspaces: In a narrow crawlspace such as an air shaft, you cannot move past other characters in the same zone – not even friendlies. Xenomorphs often prefer to move through air shafts and other crawlspaces, but can move through rooms and corridors just like human characters, including opening unlocked doors.

Dragging A Person: You can drag a broken or otherwise immobilized person with you when you move. The person needs to be at Adjacent range, and you need to make a STAMINA roll. If you fail, you remain in the zone.

Leaving Combat

You can attempt to leave a combat before it’s over by moving out of sight of your opponents. If you do, and it’s not obvious where you went (GM’s call), your opponents must roll for OBSERVATION (no action) to understand where you went. If it fails, combat is over, and stealth mode commences again (unless other PCs remain in combat).

CLOSE COMBAT

Close combat is any attack at Adjacent range, no matter what weapon is used (if any). This is a full action. Roll for CLOSE COMBAT to hit. Close combat weapons can give a modifier to your roll.

Hit: If the attack succeeds, it inflicts the weapon’s base damage on the target, plus 1 damage point for every    rolled beyond the first. Damage may be reduced by body armor (Critical Injuries ). Unarmed attacks have a base damage of 1.

Weak Spot: Against an armored target, you can aim for a weak spot, getting –2 dice. On a hit, the armor level is reduced 1 step (after reduction for an armor piercing attack).

Defend

If you are attacked in close combat, you can choose to defend yourself against the attack, to avoid being hit. Defending is a quick action, and you roll for CLOSE COMBAT. You must state that you defend before the attacker rolls for their strike. Defending turns the attack into an opposed roll (Relieving Stress ) – for each    you roll when defending, you eliminate one    rolled by the attacker.

Interruption: Defending is an interrupt action and occurs out of turn. It does require a quick action however – if you have no actions left in the round, you cannot defend. If you fear you will be attacked later in a round, it might be wise to save a quick action for a possible defense.

Special Attacks

In close combat, you may want to achieve something other than just harming your opponent. You must state that you are attempting a special attack before rolling dice, and you cannot use any bonus dice from a weapon. Special attacks can be defended against just like normal attacks. If the attack succeeds, you inflict no damage but instead achieve the desired result:

Disarm: You wrestle an item from your opponent’s grasp. You can keep the item or throw it into an adjacent zone as part of the attack.

Pass: You move past an enemy blocking your movement (Foot Movement ). If successful, place your token or miniature on the other side of the enemy.

Shove: You push your opponent to Short range from you. This attack can be used to shove your target through a door or hatch.

Grapple: Your enemy cannot move or perform any actions except trying to break free. This is a full action and an opposed CLOSE COMBAT roll against you (Xenomorphs use MOBILITY instead). While you are grappling, the only action you can perform is a grapple attack. This works as a normal unarmed attack but cannot be defended against.

Restrained & Unaware Opponents

If your close combat opponent is restrained or unaware of you (see Surprise & Ambush ), they cannot defend themselves against the attack and you get +2 dice to the roll.

Firearms In Close Combat

Note that you can use a firearm even in close combat. You still use the CLOSE COMBAT skill (not RANGED COMBAT) to hit. As most firearms have a minimum range of Short (or more), you typically get –2 dice or more when using them in close combat. Your target can defend against the attack normally.

RANGED COMBAT

When you attack someone at Short distance or more, roll for RANGED COMBAT. You need to have line of sight to your target (Zones ). You also need a ranged weapon (see the Gear table). Most ranged weapons give a modifier to your roll. Firing a weapon is a full action.

Hayes tries to defend himself against the attack. With Strength 3 and no skill level in CLOSE COMBAT, he only rolls three base dice, but with stress level 3 he also gets to add three stress dice. He gets a single   and luckily, no  .

Hit: If the attack succeeds, it inflicts the weapon’s base damage on the target, plus 1 damage point for every    rolled beyond the first. Damage may be reduced by armor.

Aiming: If you take your time to aim carefully before squeezing the trigger, you get +2 dice to your roll. Aiming is a quick action and can only be done at Short range or more. The aim must happen on your turn, immediately before the attack.

Range: Weapons have a minimum and maximum range. Any attack closer than the minimum range gets –2 dice per range band below the minimum range. This does not apply to attacks against unaware or restrained targets. A weapon cannot be used beyond its maximum range – with the exception that you can fire a weapon with Short maximum range into an adjacent zone if you’re standing right next to a door or hatch to that zone.

Nat, at Short range from the Xenomorph, raises her Rexim RXF-M5 EVA Pistol at the Xenomorph, using her quick action to aim carefully and her full action to fire.

With no skill level in RANGED COMBAT, she needs all the bonuses she can get.

She rolls six base dice (three for her Agility 3, +1 for her Rexim, and +2 for aiming) and two stress dice (her current stress level is 2), getting two   . Nat could use the extra    to conserve ammo but decides to maximize the damage. The Rexim has a base damage rating of 1, meaning the shot hits for 2 points of damage.

Weak Spot: Against an armored target, you can aim for a weak spot, getting –2 dice. On a hit, the armor level is reduced 1 step (after reduction for an armor piercing attack).

Target Size: Firing at a large target, such as a vehicle, gives +2 dice. Firing at a small object, such as a terminal screen, a hand-held item, or a Chestburster, gives −2 dice.

Dodging

If you are attacked in ranged combat, you can try to dodge the attack. This is a quick action, and you roll for MOBILITY. You can only dodge if you are aware of the attacker, and you must declare a dodge before the attacker rolls. Dodging turns the attack into an opposed roll (Opposed Rolls ) – for each    you roll when dodging, you eliminate one    rolled by the attacker.

Interruption: Dodging is an interrupt action and occurs out of turn. It does require a quick action however – if you have no actions left in the round, you cannot dodge. If you fear you will be attacked later in a round, it might be wise to save a quick action for a possible dodge.

Cover

When bullets start flying, you’ll do well to seek cover. You can only take cover in a cluttered zone, never in an open zone – except by a door or hatch, which gives you cover against enemies in the adjacent zone.. There are two types of cover – partial and full.

Partial Cover: Taking partial cover is a quick action. You expose enough of yourself to be able to see, and shoot at, your enemy. When in partial cover, any ranged attack against you gets –2 dice. You can dodge when in partial cover.

Full Cover: Completely hiding yourself from view is a full action. Full cover breaks line of sight. Ranged attacks are still possible but get –3 dice and the attacks must penetrate the barrier (Barriers ).

You cannot dodge when in full cover.

Friendly Fire

If you fire at a target Adjacent to another character and miss, you risk hitting the unintended target instead. Roll for an attack with two base dice, inflicting base damage if one    is rolled and 1 additional damage on two    . If there are several Adjacent targets, randomize which one is hit.

Ammunition

Ranged weapons require ammunition. You don’t need to count individual bullets. Instead, the ammo capacity of each weapon works as a supply rating (Consumables ). After each attack, make a supply roll for your weapon. When the ammo supply runs out, you need to reload.

Reload: Reloading a firearm is a quick action, unless stated otherwise. You need to track your available reloads on your character sheet.

Single-Shot: Weapons designated as single-shot must be reloaded after each shot – no supply roll is made.

NPCs: For NPCs, the GM doesn’t make ammo supply rolls. Instead, their ammo capacity is reduced by one step after each attack.

Full Auto

Some weapons can fire bursts of bullets. When you fire a burst and hit, without pushing the roll, you can immediately make another attack roll, at the same target or another, as part of the same action. If you hit again (without pushing), you may roll a third time. As soon as you miss, or push a roll, the attack is over. Each attack roll except the first gives you stress level +1. You cannot make more than three attack rolls in a single burst.

Ammo: When firing a burst, you must make an ammo supply roll after each attack roll.

Aiming: If you aim carefully (RANGED COMBAT ), the bonus will only apply to the first attack roll of the burst.

DAMAGE

IN COMBAT, you run the risk of being injured. Everything from exhaustion to bleeding cuts and broken bones is summarized as damage. How much damage you can take before being broken is determined by your Health score.

Armor

To protect yourself from harm, you can wear body armor. Xenomorphs often have natural body armor. The effectiveness of armor is represented by its armor level. When you take damage from an external attack, the damage caused is reduced by the armor level.

Armor Piercing: Against attacks designated as armor piercing, the armor level counts as 1 step lower than its normal value (to a minimum of zero).

Weak Spots: Attacks in both close and ranged combat can be aimed at weak spots in the armor. This gives the attack a –2 modifier, but on a hit, the armor level is reduced 1 step (in addition to any reduction for an armor piercing attack).

Barriers

Barriers such as spaceship bulkheads also have armor levels – see the adjacent table for examples. When a ranged attack hits a barrier, the damage is reduced by the armor level. If the damage is reduced to zero, the attack does not breach the barrier.

Breach Limit: For barriers (and vehicles) only, if the armor level is higher than the base damage rating of the weapon (not just equal), after any modifiers for ammunition and weak spots, the attack cannot breach the armor, no matter how many are rolled.

Cover: Note that partial cover (Cover ) does not provide an armor level – only full cover will do that. If you are in full cover behind a barrier and wear body armor, first apply the effect of the cover, then the armor.

Broken

If you drop to zero Health, you are broken – in effect, taken out of the action. Immediately roll for a critical injury. While broken, you can make a single move action per round and mumble through the pain but not perform any other actions.

You can’t go below zero Health, but any further damage gives you another critical injury. While broken, you cannot gain more stress and you never make panic rolls. There are three ways to get back up after being broken:

BROKEN NPCs

NPCs can be broken in the same ways as PCs. An NPC can rally or give first aid to a PC and vice versa. However, dice are usually not rolled when an NPC aids another NPC – instead, the GM decides what happens. The GM can also decide that a minor NPC who is broken simply dies.

  • First Aid: Someone at Adjacent range can administer first aid with a MEDICAL AID roll (full action, modified for medical gear). On a success, you are no longer broken and recover 1 point of Health per rolled. If you suffer from a lethal critical injury (below), you are also stabilized.
  • Rally: Another character in the same zone can try to rally you with a COMMAND roll (quick action). If successful, you are no longer broken and recover 1 point of Health per rolled. Rallying has no effect on critical injuries.
  • On Your Own: If you’re broken (but not dead) and no one gives you first aid, you automatically get back up after one stretch of time and recover 1 point of Health.

Recovery: As long as you are not fatigued (Fatigue ), you automatically recover 1 point of Health per stretch of time while resting in a safe area (even if suffering from a critical injury). First aid and rallying can only recover Health when you are broken.

Critical Injuries

When you are reduced to zero Health, roll a D6 on the table below. If you roll a critical injury that you already have (result #3 or above), re-roll.

Death: If you suffer a critical injury listed as lethal, you must make a death roll after the listed time limit has passed. If the time limit is round, roll on your every turn, right after you act. A death roll is a roll for STAMINA (not an action), but you cannot push it, and you are not allowed to roll any stress dice. If you fail a death roll, you die. If you succeed, you linger on, but you must make another death roll when the listed time limit has passed again.

First Aid: To save your life when you have suffered a lethal critical injury, someone must give you first aid before you fail a death roll. This is a full action and requires a MEDICAL AID roll, modified for medical gear. If you are no longer broken, you can try to administer first aid on yourself, but with −2 dice.

HANDLING DEATH

The death of a PC can be traumatic but try not to see it as a failure. Instead, consider it a dramatic peak in your story and then get back into the action as soon as possible. In cinematic adventures, character deaths are quite common – and can be very memorable events in the story.

ADVANCED CRITS

The full ALIEN RPG Core Rulebook includes a more comprehensive list of critical injuries. If you have access to this and prefer more detailed results, you can use it even when playing Hope’s Last Day.

Xenomorphs: Note that there are some Xenomorph signature attacks that kill you outright. If you roll any of these, you’re dead. No death rolls, no chance of surviving – you’re done for.

Wounded: If you suffer critical injury #3 or worse, you are Wounded. When Wounded, movement in combat becomes a full action for D6 days. There is a card for this in this boxed set.

PANIC

Being in the cold darkness of space will test your nerves even under normal circumstances. Add horrifying Xenomorphs, and you really need to keep your nerves in check to avoid spiraling into a wild panic.

Stress Level

The mounting tension in your character is measured by your stress level. It starts at zero and increases during the course of the game. Your stress can increase in many ways, such as:

  • You push a skill roll (Pushing Your Roll ).
  • You or a nearby PC suffers a certain stress or panic response.
  • A nearby NPC panics (as determined by the GM).
  • You make a second or third attack roll in a burst of full auto fire (Full Auto ).
  • You become fatigued (Full Auto ).
  • A member of your own crew attacks you.
  • Any unnerving encounter as determined by the adventure or the GM.
  1. Roll D6.
  2. Add your stress level.
  3. Subtract your Resolve.
  4. Check the panic response table.

Panic Roll

As long as you keep your stress in check, you can use it to your advantage. But if the tension grows too strong it can explode, sending you into a wild panic. You need to make a panic roll when:

  • You witness another PC become broken.
  • You see a horrifying Xenomorph for the first time.
  • A terrifying Xenomorph comes within Adjacent range (even if you have seen it before).
  • You witness another PC suffer from a certain panic response.
  • A truly horrifying event occurs, as determined by the adventure or the GM.

Resolution: Roll a D6, add your current stress level, subtract your Resolve rating, and compare the result to the table on the next page.

More Panic: If you are suffering from a panic response and are forced to make another panic roll, you suffer both responses if possible. In cases where two responses cannot be combined, the higher response takes precedence. If you already have a panic response (or stress response of the same name) and roll the same again, use the next higher response on the table. >

On your next turn and subsequent turns, you must spend all your actions to continue to move away, until you find a (reasonably) safe place, where you must remain until your panic stops. You cannot perform interrupt actions before then.
If you cannot move out of your zone, you become Catatonic (result #12) instead.
11   Frenzy. You immediately attack the nearest person or creature, friendly or not. Every friendly PC in the zone must make an immediate panic roll. You won’t stop until you or the target is broken, or until your panic stops. You cannot perform interrupt actions before then.
12+   Catatonic. You’re doomed! You collapse to the floor and can’t move, rambling or staring blankly into oblivion, until your panic stops.

Stopping Panic

Some panic responses are immediate or last until your next turn. If this is not the case, the effect remains until one of the following happens:

  • Another character within speaking range (including comms) makes a COMMAND roll. This is a full action in combat.
  • You are broken.
  • One stretch passes.

Relieving Stress

For every stretch of time (5–10 minutes) spent resting in a safe area, your stress level is reduced by 1 point. In addition, one Stress Response of your choice is removed for each stress level reduced. You can’t make skill rolls when resting, and if your rest is interrupted, it doesn’t count. A panic roll can also decrease stress.

OTHER HAZARDS

The world of ALIEN is unforgiving, and there are many ways for your character to suffer and die.

Fatigue

If you don’t get enough air, water, food, or sleep, or if you are exposed to extreme cold or heat without adequate protection, you must make SURVIVAL rolls at regular intervals. As soon as you fail such a roll, you become fatigued. Mark this on your character sheet. There is also a card summarizing the effects in this boxed set. Being fatigued has several effects:

  • li ou can no longer recover Health.
  • You must continue to make SURVIVAL rolls at the same intervals. For each failed roll, you suffer 1 point of damage and gain +1 stress level.
  • If broken by damage from fatigue, don’t roll for a critical injury. Instead, make death rolls (for STAMINA) at the same interval as the SURVIVAL rolls. First aid has no effect against these rolls – only removing the source of the fatigue will stop the death rolls.

The Hope’s Last Day adventure will indicate if and when you risk being fatigued.

Falling

Falling on a hard surface in gravity automatically inflicts an amount of damage to you equal to the height of the fall (in meters) divided by 2, rounding all fractions down. In a controlled jump, roll MOBILITY – each rolled reduces the damage done by 1. Body armor does not protect you.

Explosions

Some weapons have an explosive effect. You fire these as a normal ranged attack, but if you hit your target, all other characters in the same zone (PC and NPCs alike) suffer the same damage. Each target can dodge the attack separately. If your attack misses, the shot is assumed to have gone astray and hurts no one.

Cover: For the primary target, cover has the same effect as in any ranged attack. Secondary targets in partial cover count as if they were in full cover (i.e. they get protection from the full armor level of the barrier).

Contained Spaces: If you fire an explosive weapon into a zone with only blocked borders (via a hatch or door from an adjacent zone, or inside the zone behind cover), you get +2 dice to the attack.

Fire

A fire typically covers one zone and is measured by its intensity. A typical fire has intensity 6–9. When entering a burning zone, or starting a round in one, roll a number of base dice equal to the intensity. For every rolled, you suffer 1 point of damage. Armor has its normal effect.

If you are broken by fire damage, don’t roll for a critical injury – instead, make a death roll every round until you’re out of the fire.

Catching Fire: If you take damage from a fire attack, you catch fire and continue to burn, suffering another fire attack at the start of each new round even if you leave the burning zone. As soon as a fire attack outside the burning zone inflicts no damage, you’re no longer on fire. You, or a friend at Adjacent range, can stop you from burning with a successful MOBILITY roll (full action).

Fire Spreading: For a typical fire, roll a D6 at the start of each round. On 1–2, the fire goes out and the zone is no longer considered burning. On a 5–6, the fire spreads to a random adjacent zone, assuming the zone border is open and there is something in the adjacent zone that can burn.

D6   EFFECT
1-2   The fire goes out.
3-4   The fire continues to burn.
5-6   The fire spreads to a random adjacent zone, if the zone border is open and there is flammable material in the zone.

Synthetics

In combat, androids act like humans, and they make skill rolls normally. But there are several differences:

Attributes: Synthetics generally have higher attribute levels than humans.

Skills & Stress: Androids can’t push skill rolls. They don’t suffer stress, don’t have a stress level, and they never make panic rolls.

Damage: If a synthetic goes to zero Health, don’t roll for a critical injury. Instead, roll for critical systems damage on the table below. Until the android suffers a system shutdown (result #6), it can continue to operate, only suffering the effects of the critical injury. This makes androids very hard to stop.

1   Ruptured Fluid Pump. The android loses its next turn, and cannot perform interrupt actions until then.

3   Destroyed Arm Servos. One arm is non-functional. The android can only use one-handed gear.
4   Head Dislocation. The android’s artificial neck is severely fractured and its head placed in an unnatural position. All quick actions become full actions.
5   Severe Chassis Breach. Internal components spill out and the android is completely immobilized.
6   System Shutdown. The android is torn to shreds or crushed beyond repair. Core systems are severely damaged and a COMTECH roll is required to communicate with the android.
